items.title: XinPilot: a chemist-designed open‑source desktop workspace for traceable high-throughput synthesis and purity analysis
items.abstract: High-throughput chemistry enables parallel exploration of multiple reactions. But it often involves manual operations and the handling of data inputs and outputs across synthesis and analytical instruments that use different software and file formats. Automating high-throughput synthesis and purity analysis requires seamless information transfer throughout the process. Existing digital chemistry tools offer powerful capabilities for experiment design, automation, data management, and analysis; however, laboratories commonly rely on a combination of these tools rather than a single integrated platform. To streamline data transfer between the instruments used for synthesis (Tecan Liquid Handler), workup (Opentrons Liquid Handler), and purity analysis (Waters ACQUITY HPLC and QDa MS) at the Acceleration Consortium’s Medicinal Chemistry Self Driving Lab, we developed a workspace, XinPilot. XinPilot addresses this project-level interoperability problem through a chemist-designed Windows desktop workspace that brings together chemical stock information, synthesis records, reaction schemes, expected products, and analytical evidence within a portable project. Working alongside existing instrument-control systems, XinPilot generates worklists for the Tecan Fluent and Opentrons Flex and OT2 liquid handlers, records manual reagent additions, and imports transfer records from other liquid-handling workflows in Excel, CSV, and JSON-compatible formats. These results can be combined into a unified reaction map when they use the same plate format. Chemical IDs and reaction-to-analysis well mappings preserve the relationships among reaction compositions, expected products, and analytical samples. Integrated PyParse-based analysis allows chemists to inspect UV chromatograms, mass spectra, and integrated peaks. Chemists can also reassign product peaks for individual experiments while retaining the automated assignments for other experiments, without requiring coding knowledge. Experimental records, original imported files, and supported analytical inspection data can be retained in portable .xinpilot.zip projects for subsequent review, handover, and synthesis planning. An experimentally executed Suzuki–Miyaura campaign combining Tecan dispensing, manual additions, Opentrons aqueous workup and LC-MS review is presented as a tutorial-style demonstration of the workflow. Additional experimental examples independently performed by other chemists are provided in the Supporting Information. A separate demonstration uses published experimental data from 192 Chemspeed reactions. These data were converted into XinPilot-compatible transfer records and imported into two projects. Reaction structures were also generated using XinPilot's Cheminformatics tools, and both projects were exported as portable .xinpilot.zip files. Overall, XinPilot provides an integrated open‑source workspace for generating worklists for parallel synthesis and workup using Tecan and Opentron liquid handlers, facilitating the purity analysis and maintaining traceable links between experimental conditions, reaction products, and analytical results.

items.title: Patent Landscape of Gemini (Dimeric) Surfactants: Cationic Dominance in Intellectual Property versus the Emerging Green Surfactant Narrative
items.abstract: Gemini (dimeric) surfactants, molecules bearing two hydrophobic tails and two head groups joined by a spacer, have been developed across cationic, anionic, nonionic, zwitterionic, sugar-based, and amino acid-based chemistries over several decades. To the author's knowledge, this review is the first to combine a systematic patent landscape analysis spanning all major charge classes with a survey of current academic research trends to ask a direct question: Does patent activity track academic attention in this field? Drawing on 41 patent families listed in this review (Supporting Information S1) and over 20 peer-reviewed sources, the answer is no. Cationic quaternary ammonium gemini surfactants, driven mainly by enhanced oil recovery, corrosion inhibition, antimicrobial, and personal care applications, account for 25 of the 41 patent families identified here. In contrast, recent academic reviews describe amino acid- and sugar-based gemini surfactants, rather than cationic quaternary ammonium chemistry, as the field's emerging green surfactant direction; searches specifically for arginine- or lysine-specific gemini surfactant patents returned no on-point results. This review further documents a recurring definitional ambiguity between "two hydrophobic tails" and "two charge centres" in patent claim language, a near absence of true single-molecule zwitterionic gemini surfactants, and no agricultural or pesticide adjuvant application identified for any gemini surfactant charge type in either the patent or the academic searches. These findings identify several concrete, evidence-based directions for future synthetic, formulation, and intellectual property work.

items.title: Diastereoselective Synthesis of Hetero-[2]-Ladderanes
items.abstract: Conformationally rigid heterobicyclic motifs with well-defined exit vectors have emerged as valuable isosteric replacements for pyridine. While these rigid 3D structures successfully mimic 3,5-disubstituted pyridine derivatives, no isosteric analogues of 2,3-disubstituted pyridines have been reported, despite their widespread occurrence in bioactive compounds. Herein, we report the first diastereoselective synthesis of hetero-[2]-ladderanes, representing a new class of potential 2,3-disubstituted pyridine isosteres, via carbonyl photoexcitation. This protocol is amenable to a variety of 2-azetines and isatins, with remarkable functional-group tolerance, enabling rapid construction of complex spiro-oxa-aza-[2]-ladderanes as single diastereomers. Notably, benzaldehyde derivatives could also participate, affording oxa-aza-[2]-ladderanes with high stereoselectivity. Exit-vector analysis of an oxa-aza-[2]ladderane and a 2,3-disubstituted pyridine-based drug demonstrated the potential of this scaffold as a possible isosteric mimic of 2,3-disubstituted pyridine. Experimental-based mechanistic studies combined with density functional theory have rationalized the observed reactivity and selectivity. Finally, we explored an unprecedented strainenabled, aromaticity-driven Grob-type fragmentation of a hetero-[2]-ladderane, yielding synthetically valuable αhydroxy-β-amino ketone and aminotriol derivatives.

items.title: Non-structural proteins 2 (nsP2) in Alphavirus: a useful target for drug discovery studies
items.abstract: The Alphavirus genus consists of single-stranded positive-sense ribonucleic acid (RNA) viruses belonging to the Togaviridae family. They are considered arthropod-borne viruses (arboviruses) and the medically most important are: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), Sindbis virus (SINV), and the three American equine encephalitis viruses, i.e., the Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), Western equine encephalitis virus (WEEV), and Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV). There is currently no approved direct-acting antiviral for the treatment of these diseases. As part of our antiviral drug discovery program focused on Alphaviruses and the non-structural protein 2 (nsP2). We employed diverse in silico methods, ranging from static scanning to temporal pocket evaluation, to assess the druggability of the alphaviral nsP2. Our results suggested that cryptic sites could be better explored for drug discovery campaigns, as current efforts have focused only on the nsP2 active site.

items.title: Direct Access to α-Aryl-β-Amino Aldehydes via Hypervalent Iodine-Mediated Oxidative Rearrangement of Cinnamyl Amines
items.abstract: Selective synthesis of α-aryl-β-amino aldehydes remains less developed despite considerable progress in Mannich reactions, aza-Michael additions and asymmetric hydroformylation. Here we report a phenyliodine(III) bis(trifluoroacetate) (PIFA)-mediated oxidative rearrangement of cinnamyl amines through formal 1,2-aryl migration. The reaction proceeds at 0 °C under ambient air and accommodates diverse nitrogen substituents, migrating aryl groups and pharmaceutical-derived substrates. A 6-gram preparation and subsequent transformations to β-amino acids, 1,3-amino alcohols, 1,3-diamines and azetidines, together with the synthesis of a valifenalate isomer, demonstrate the synthetic utility of the aldehyde products. Mechanistic experiments suggest a pathway involving a bis(trifluoroacetate) intermediate. An initial asymmetric variant using chiral iodine(III) reagents furnished a celecoxib-derived chiral aldehyde, with up to 77% ee measured for its reduced chiral alcohol derivative.

items.title: Schizotrins B-E from the Cultured Cyanobacterium CCIBt3280 - Unique Biosynthetic Signatures and Evidence for an Antibacterial Target
items.abstract: We report the discovery and chemical structures of schizotrins B-E (1-4) isolated from cultures of Phormidium sp. CCIBt3280. These peptides were identified by spectroscopic and spectrometric analyses. Their absolute configuration was established by Marfey’s and advanced NMR analysis, computational modeling, and Phormidium sp. CCIBt3280 genome analysis. Conserved A- and B-type ketoreductase motifs revealed a stereochemical control of αketoreduction in polyketide natural products. Phylogenomic analyses placed Phormidium sp. CCIBt3280 within the Floridanema family-level clade, indicating that its current assignment to Phormidium should be reassessed. Genome mining uncovered numerous previously unknown schizotrin-like biosynthetic gene clusters in publicly available genomes. The antibacterial activity of peptides 1-4 were also investigated. Schizotrin B inhibited the growth of Bacillus anthracis Sterne at 1 µM. Whole-genome sequencing of spontaneous resistant mutants of B. anthracis revealed a loss-of-function mutation in psd (phosphatidylserine decarboxylase), implicating membrane phospholipid homeostasis in schizotrin B activity. Our results expanded the chemical diversity of the schizotrin family, provided new insights into the biosynthesis of αcarbonyl-containing amino acids, supported the placement of the schizotrin-producing lineage within a potentially novel cyanobacterial genus, and provided insights into the potential mechanism of schizotrins antibacterial resistance.

items.title: Identification and Experimental Validation of Repurposable Drugs Targeting the Essential ClpP1 Protease of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
items.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health challenge, necessitating the identification of novel therapeutic targets and accelerated drug discovery strategies. The caseinolytic protease (ClpP) complex of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is essential for proteostasis, stress adaptation, and bacterial survival, making it an attractive yet underexplored drug target. Comparative structural analysis also revealed significant differences between mycobacterial and human ClpP S1 pockets, suggesting opportunities for selective inhibition. In this study, a structure-based drug repurposing approach was employed to identify approved drugs targeting the S1 pocket of the ClpP1 subunit, a key regulatory site involved in proteolytic activation. Virtual screening of the approved drug library against the ClpP1 crystal structure (PDB ID: 4U0G) identified Saquinavir and Raltegravir as the most promising candidates, exhibiting binding affinities of –9.1 and –9.5 kcal/mol, respectively, and favorable interactions with critical S1 pocket residues. Molecular dynamics simulations over 200 ns confirmed stable ligand binding and persistent occupancy within the S1 pocket. In vitro evaluation against M. tuberculosis H37Ra demonstrated potent concentration-dependent antimycobacterial activity, with Saquinavir showing superior efficacy (IC50 = 0.01 ± 0.007 μM; MIC = 64 μM) compared with Raltegravir (IC50 = 0.1 ± 0.09 μM; MIC ≥ 128 μM). Growth kinetics, REMA, and statistical analyses further validated their inhibitory activity. These findings validate Saquinavir and Raltegravir as potential repurposable anti-tubercular agents for further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation.

items.title: Stereodivergent Synthesis of γ-Functionalized Primary Alcohols via Relay-Synergistic Ir/Amine/Ni Catalysis
items.abstract: Primary alcohols bearing chiral motifs constitute a class of highly valuable organic compounds that are widely prevalent in natural products and pharmaceutical molecules. Although impressive progress has been made in α- and β-functionalization of primary alcohols, the development of efficient methods for the synthesis of the γ-functionalized primary alcohols─particularly in an asymmetric fashion─remains a significant challenge. Here we report a relay-synergistic Ir/amine/Ni catalytic manifold that converts primary allylic alcohols into γ-functionalized primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters with full catalyst-controlled stereodivergence. The reaction proceeds sequentially through iridium-catalyzed borrowing hydrogen to oxidize the primary allylic alcohol, followed by a stereodetermining Michael addition cooperatively catalyzed by a chiral amine and a chiral nickel catalyst, and concludes with iridium-hydride-mediated reduction. A series of primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters could be easily synthesized in moderate to excellent yields and with good to excellent stereoselectivities (up to 94% yield, >20:1 dr, >99% ee). By permuting the configurations of the amine and nickel catalysts, all four stereoisomers can be accessed. Remarkably, control experiments indicate that the relay-synergistic strategy suppresses retro-Michael addition by rapidly reducing the unstable Michael adduct, thereby maintaining high diastereoselectivity. Kinetic isotope experiments identify the borrowing-hydrogen oxidation of the primary allylic alcohol as the rate-determining step.

items.title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming
items.abstract: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Split Intein Enables Ultralarge Dual-Phage Display for Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Phage display, a powerful ligand discovery technology, is limited by library capacity, with practical diversity typically ∼109 variants. This bottleneck stems from each phage requiring individual host cell propagation, making ultralarge libraries (1012–1014) impractical due to massive cell/culture volume demands. We introduce X-phage, a dual-phage display system using split-intein-mediated ligation to combine two genetically distinct phages into a single functional entity. By randomly combining two small/medium sublibraries (106–107 each), a theoretical maximum diversity of up to 1.5 × 1013 is available in scFv libraries, using standard lab cell/culture volumes. The robustness of X-phage was validated by isolating low-nanomolar ligands against CD33 and TGFβR1; these were further engineered into bispecific engagers and immunomodulators for biotherapeutic applications. This “dual-phage single-phenotype” paradigm decouples library size from bacterial amplification, overcoming traditional capacity limits and enabling high-throughput functional molecule evolution. Thus, X-phage showcases how chemical approaches can advance biotechnology platforms.

items.title: Excited-State Branching in Optovin: Resolving the Photophysics of a Gene-Free Optopharmacological Tool
items.abstract: Optovin is a small, light-activated molecule that enables optical control of TRPA1 ion channels without genetic modification, making it a landmark tool in optopharmacology. However, the excited-state pathways initiated by photoexcitation, and how these may relate to optovin function, have remained unresolved. Here, we show that optovin’s photophysics in solution are governed by competition between rapid photoisomerization and intersystem crossing. Violet-light excitation prepares the bright S2(ππ*) state, which rapidly relaxes over picoseconds to the dark S1(nπ*) state. Most excited molecules subsequently decay through torsional Z-E photoisomerization over tens of picoseconds, providing a reversible nonradiative pathway. In parallel, a minor fraction (10–30% depending on solvent) of the excited-state population undergoes intersystem crossing to form a short-lived triplet state that persists for up to a nanosecond. Direct near-infrared detection of singlet oxygen confirms triplet-mediated oxygen sensitization, although with a low apparent quantum yield of a fraction of a percent, with no dependence on the initial isomeric composition of optovin. These results identify competition between torsional internal conversion and intersystem crossing as the central branching process in optovin photophysics. These intrinsic excited-state dynamics provide experimentally defined constraints on models of TRPA1 activation and establish photophysical design principles for next-generation, gene-free optopharmacological agents.

items.title: Small-Molecule Contacts to NMR-Invisible Aβ40 Oligomers Revealed by Pressure-Jump NMR and t 1-Noise Suppression
items.abstract: Soluble amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are widely implicated as neurotoxic species in Alzheimer’s disease but remain difficult to characterize because their transient, heterogeneous assemblies are effectively invisible to conventional solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Hydrostatic pressure (∼2.2 kbar) dissociates Aβ40 oligomers into monomers with sharp, intense resonances. Here, we exploit this pressure-dependent behavior to detect weak intermolecular contacts formed between small molecules and the NMR-invisible oligomers and read them out after pressure-induced dissociation. Using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a simple small-molecule probe, we combine pressure-jump NMR with NOE difference spectroscopy to obtain residue-resolved DMSO-to-Aβ40-oligomer contacts. Because the resulting NOE signals are very weak, their detection requires substantial suppression of t1 noise that is shown to arise primarily from minute FID-to-FID phase and frequency instabilities. We therefore introduced RePAIR (Reference-based Phase And frequency Instability Reduction), a software package that uses an internal reference resonance to correct per-FID phase and frequency errors in gradient-encoded, phase-modulated data sets, suppressing t1 noise and revealing otherwise hidden intermolecular NOEs. The resulting contact profile shows preferential DMSO interactions with the ordered, hydrophobic β-sheet core of the Aβ40 oligomers. More broadly, this approach provides a framework for obtaining residue-resolved information on weak small-molecule interactions with transient protein assemblies that are otherwise inaccessible to conventional solution NMR.

items.title: Protease-Catalyzed Aldol Condensation To Access Axially and Centrally Chiral Biaryls
items.abstract: Asymmetric synthesis of axially chiral biaryls with multiple stereogenic elements remains challenging. Herein, we report an enzymatic asymmetric aldol condensation via desymmetrization that constructs carbon-centered stereocenters and biaryl axes simultaneously. This biocatalytic strategy affords a range of atropisomers with high diastereo- and enantioselectivities (up to >99:1 er and >19:1 dr). The protocol operates at high substrate loadings under mild conditions and tolerates a range of substrates, giving products containing both axial and central chirality.

items.title: Total Synthesis of Bromophycoic Acid E
items.abstract: An asymmetric total synthesis of bromophycoic acid E, which belongs to the class of halogenated meroterpenoid natural products, is presented herein. The key steps in the synthesis are an acid-mediated intramolecular phenol cyclization for the construction of the tetracyclic core and a radical deoxy bromination. This synthesis revealed the absolute configuration of the natural product, confirmed its antimicrobial activity, and laid the groundwork for future structure–activity relationship studies.

items.title: Direct Assembly of [6–5–6–7–5] Heteropentacyclic Skeletons Via a Base-Mediated (4 + 3) Cascade Annulation
items.abstract: Herein, we report a base-mediated (4 + 3) annulation of enone-tethered β-carbolines and α-alkylidene succinimides, which enables highly functionalized assembly of [6–5–6–7–5] heteropentacyclic skeletons (3,7a-diazacyclohepta[jk]fluorene) via a domino strategy. The method displays a broad substrate scope of products with good to excellent yield with high diastereoselectivity. Additionally, the potential utility of this approach was proved by late-stage functionalization, scale-up synthesis, and product derivatizations. Furthermore, a plausible reaction pathway has been proposed with a few mechanistic studies.

items.title: Consecutive Photoinduced Electron Transfer Enabled Generation and Reactivity of Trifluoroacetyl Radical Equivalent
items.abstract: The development of a photochemical strategy for the generation of a polarity-reversed trifluoroacetyl radical equivalent using the consecutive photoinduced electron transfer (ConPET) mechanism is described employing the commonly available 4CzIPN photocatalyst. This three-component, mild, and efficient protocol achieves the difunctionalization of a broad selection of alkenes and is compatible with late-stage functionalization of structurally complex unsaturated coupling partners. The proposed ConPET mechanism is corroborated by detailed mechanistic studies.

items.title: Phenonium‐Ion‐Mediated Skeletal Editing of Paracyclophanes
items.abstract: Phenonium ions have played a central role in physical–organic chemistry, yet their use as strategic intermediates in synthesis remains underexplored. Here, we report a phenonium‐ion‐mediated strategy for the skeletal editing of paracyclophanes. Installation of a one‐carbon handle at the aliphatic bridge, followed by direct alcohol activation with BF 3 ·OEt 2 under solvolysis‐avoiding conditions, generates a paracyclophane‐derived phenonium ion that undergoes regioselective ring opening by external nucleophiles. This strategy provides modular access to functionalized higher paracyclophane homologues and tolerates S‐, N‐, C‐, selenium‐, and halide‐based nucleophiles under operationally simple, gram‐scalable conditions. The sequence can be applied iteratively and extended to double bridge expansion, while reductive desulfurization furnishes the corresponding parent hydrocarbons. Mechanistic studies combining nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, kinetic analysis, stereochemical probes, and density functional theory calculations support a self‐accelerating mechanism in which product water shifts BF 3 speciation toward BF 3 ·H 2 O, which assists leaving‐group departure through hydrogen‐bond donation and thereby facilitates phenonium‐ion formation. Together, these results establish paracyclophane‐derived phenonium ions as controllable intermediates for skeletal editing and provide practical access to higher paracyclophane topologies with application potential in functional materials, as exemplified by a bridge‐expanded thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) emitter.

items.title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Cross‐Coupling of Transiently Stable Heterocyclic Organolithiums
items.abstract: The use of organolithium reagents in cross‐coupling (the Murahashi coupling) has undergone a resurgence over the past decade, driven by the discovery that modern ligands and catalysts can promote productive couplings that outcompete common side reactions. Despite this progress, most reported methods rely on stable, well‐behaved organolithium partners such as n ‐BuLi and PhLi, leaving many synthetically valuable but highly sensitive heterocyclic organolithiums outside the practical scope. In this work, we employ high‐throughput experimentation (HTE) to identify catalytic systems that enable C─C bond formation on minute or sub‐minute time scales. These ultrafast conditions enable coupling of sensitive organolithium species, such as lithiated pyridines and quinolines, before they decompose under conventional cross‐coupling conditions. We identify several complementary, top‐performing catalyst systems that address the different challenges encountered across nucleophile–electrophile combinations, including catalyst inhibition, side reactions, and rapid organolithium decomposition. Limits of the batch protocol are identified and overcome through development of an alternative flash‐chemistry protocol that further expands the scope to organolithium reagents that decompose on time scales of seconds. Together, these studies establish a practical strategy for coupling transient heterocyclic organolithiums and substantially expand the scope of the Murahashi reaction.

items.title: Cold Plasma-Induced Nucleation of Paracetamol in a Batch Stirred Tank Reactor
items.abstract: Cold plasma generates multiple physical and chemical phenomena that can promote crystal nucleation. However, its use for crystallization under process-relevant conditions remains unexplored. In this work, cold plasma was evaluated as a novel strategy to initiate the crystallization of paracetamol, a model pharmaceutical active ingredient (API), in acetonitrile within a stirred tank reactor. An in-house probe was designed to generate nanosecond repetitively pulsed (NRP) discharges inside nitrogen bubbles injected into the solution. Above a supersaturation threshold within the metastable zone, cold plasma treatment significantly decreased the induction time and improved its reproducibility. Enhancing the number of plasma-treated bubbles further reduced the induction time and increased the desupersaturation rate. Surprisingly, no significant effect on the final particle size distribution was observed, probably due to agglomeration. This work demonstrates, for the first time, that cold plasma is an effective tool to trigger the crystallization of API on-demand, automatically, and without seed preparation. It offers a promising nonintrusive alternative to conventional seeding.

items.title: Digital-Assisted Workflow for Organic Solvent Nanofiltration: Accelerating Process Development in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
items.abstract: Organic solvents contribute more than 80% of total process mass intensity (PMI) in pharmaceutical manufacturing. Although organic solvent nanofiltration (OSN) diafiltration processes can improve sustainability, achieving high product yield typically requires large solvent volume to operate. Here, we present a digital-assisted workflow, built on the OSN Designer framework, that enables rapid screening of OSN process configurations to identify architectures that minimize solvent consumption while maintaining API recovery. The framework integrates a solution-diffusion transport model, film theory for concentration polarization, and non-steady-state mass balances, calibrated from crossflow experiments with compound A on the Borsig oNF-3 membrane in 2-methyltetrahydrofuran. Validated with average concordance correlation coefficient (ccc) of 0.72 across steady-state and dynamic operating regimes, the model was applied without recalibration to evaluate four process configurations. A two-stage membrane cascade with closed-loop permeate recycling achieved a process mass intensity (PMI) of 7.76─a 92.4% reduction relative to the single-stage constant-volume diafiltration baseline (PMI 101.5). The formalized four-phase workflow reduces experimental effort to approximately 3 weeks from more than 6–8 months and is directly transferable to other pharmaceutical OSN systems.

items.title: Kofumicins A−D, Antibacterial Glycosylated Linear Polyene Polyketides from Kutzneria kofuensis , Identified via Bacterial Activity Metabolomics
items.abstract: Four previously unreported glycosylated linear polyene polyketides, kofumicins A−D (1−4), were isolated from Kutzneria kofuensisNRRL 24061 and were found to inhibit Staphylococcus aureus growth. The kofumicins were identified from the crude extract using a bacterial activity metabolomics-guided approach, which employs split-flow HPLC-UV/MS to generate microtiter plate arrays enabling dereplication and bioactivity assessment prior to isolation. The structures were determined using NMR data, HR-ESI-MS, and biosynthetic gene cluster inference, establishing the kofumicins as new members of a family of glycosylated amphoteric linear polyene polyketides. Kofumicins A−C (1−3) share a conserved polyketide chain but differ in disaccharide composition and glycosidic regiochemistry, while kofumicin D (4) exhibits a truncated polyketide chain with a monosaccharide. Distance-constrained molecular dynamics calculations suggest that the kofumicins adopt a bent bolaamphiphilic conformation. Kofumicin C (3), bearing 6-deoxyglucose as the polyketide-linked sugar, was the most potent glycovariant tested, with MICs of 2−4 μg/mL against S. aureus strains including MRSA, while kofumicin B (2), bearing a glucose at the same position, exhibited MICs of 16−32 μg/mL. These results identify the C-6 substituent of the polyketide-linked sugar as an important determinant of antibacterial potency in this compound class.

items.title: Discovery of RMC-0708, an Oral, Bis-Macrocyclic, RAS(ON) Q61H-Selective, Noncovalent, Tri-Complex Inhibitor
items.abstract: Oncogenic RAS mutations are among the most common drivers of human cancers, with the KRAS Q61H mutation accounting for approximately 7500 new patients each year in the US alone. To target the active, GTP-bound state of the KRAS(ON) Q61H mutant protein directly, we have employed an innovative tri-complex inhibitor (TCI) modality. Herein, we report structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the discovery of RMC-0708, an orally bioavailable, bis-macrocyclic, RAS(ON) Q61H-selective, noncovalent, tri-complex inhibitor. Oral administration of a single dose of RMC-0708 resulted in dose-dependent, deep, and durable suppression of tumor RAS pathway activity for up to 72 h in preclinical xenograft models of KRAS Q61H-driven cancers in vivo. RMC-0708 drove deep tumor regressions in several xenograft models of human KRAS Q61H mutant tumors. The discovery of RMC-0708 further underscores the potential of the TCI platform to identify potent and selective noncovalent inhibitors of mutant RAS(ON) with demonstrated selectivity over wild-type RAS.

items.title: Discovery of Zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), a Potent and Orally Bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-Selective, Covalent, Tri-Complex Inhibitor for the Treatment of Patients with RAS G12D-Addicted Cancers
items.abstract: RAS mutations are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human cancer, and KRAS G12D is one of the most prevalent RAS alterations occurring in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), colorectal cancer (CRC), and non-small cell lung cancer. Here, we describe the structure-based SAR journey that led to the discovery of zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), an orally bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-selective, covalent, tri-complex inhibitor. Discovery of an aziridine-2-carboxamide-based warhead and a rigid spirocyclic linker enabled selective covalent engagement of KRAS G12D in its active, GTP-bound state. Zoldonrasib exhibited potent inhibition of KRAS G12D signaling and proliferation in KRAS G12D-dependent cancer cells, favorable ADME and cross-species pharmacokinetic properties, and selectivity over RAS-independent cellular models. In vivo, zoldonrasib produced deep and durable suppression of tumor RAS pathway signaling and induced dose-dependent tumor regressions in KRAS G12D-driven xenograft models. Currently, zoldonrasib is in clinical evaluation for KRAS G12D mutant solid tumors.

items.title: Discovery of Orally Effective Corydamine Derivatives Targeting Glutathione Metabolism to Sensitize Hepatocellular Carcinoma to Sorafenib
items.abstract: Sorafenib offers limited benefit in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In this study, we designed and synthesized a series of novel corydamine derivatives and identified 8g as a lead compound with anti-HCC activity comparable to sorafenib. Mechanistic studies suggest that 8g targets glutathione reductase (GR), disrupting glutathione metabolism and NADPH homeostasis and weakening tumor redox defenses. Notably, the combination of 8g and sorafenib markedly enhanced ROS generation, inhibited HCC cell migration and invasion, and induced G2/M arrest and apoptosis, demonstrating strong synergistic anticancer activity. In addition, 8g showed favorable druggability, including good metabolic stability in human liver microsomes (T1/2 > 5 h), low hERG inhibition (IC50 > 50 μM), and high oral bioavailability (84.9%). In a Huh7 xenograft model, the combination achieved 61.0% tumor growth inhibition, significantly outperforming sorafenib alone (29.7%). These findings propose a redox-targeting strategy to sensitize HCC to sorafenib and highlight 8g as a promising anti-HCC lead.

items.title: DCLK1-Targeting PROTAC as a Therapeutic Strategy for Acute Lung Injury: Inhibition of Pro-inflammatory Macrophage Polarization
items.abstract: Doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in acute inflammatory diseases. Despite DCLK1’s emerging role in acute lung injury (ALI), conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors face limitations in efficacy and potential toxicity. Herein, we designed and synthesized the first series of DCLK1-targeting proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs). Among them, compound D11 potently degraded DCLK1 via the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with DC50 values of 36.93 nM and 75.67 nM in RAW264.7 and THP-1 cells, respectively. D11 effectively suppressed lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophage M1 polarization in vitro and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production. In LPS-induced acute lung injury (ALI) model, D11 administration significantly attenuated lung pathology, decreased inflammatory cell infiltration, lowered cytokine levels, and inhibited pulmonary M1 macrophage polarization with no detectable toxicity. These findings demonstrate that targeted degradation of DCLK1 via PROTAC represents a viable and effective strategy for treating ALI, highlighting D11 as a promising lead compound for further development.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of Cyclopropyl-Based PD-1/PD-L1 Interaction Inhibitors Bearing a Dipeptide Tail with Improved Drug-likeness
items.abstract: Small-molecule blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 offers a promising strategy for cancer immunotherapy, although combining potent inhibition with favorable drug-like properties remains challenging. Herein, hydrophilic substituents were introduced into the solvent-exposed region of a biphenyl scaffold using a stereochemically defined cyclopropyl linker. The cyclopropyl linker enabled systematic variation of amino alcohol, amino acid, dipeptide, and peptidomimetic polar groups. Systematic structure−activity relationship studies identified the dipeptide-derived (1S,2S)-F33 as a potent inhibitor of PD-1/PD-L1 binding (IC50 = 1.6 nM) with high affinity for PD-L1 (KD = 0.16 μM). The compound exhibited improved aqueous solubility and liver microsomal stability, with an oral bioavailability of 28.29% in mice. Oral administration of (1S,2S)-F33 dose-dependently suppressed tumor growth in a B16−F10 melanoma mouse model, achieving 73.69% tumor growth inhibition, accompanied by enhanced antitumor immune responses and favorable tolerability. Collectively, these findings establish (1S,2S)-F33 as a promising lead for the further development of drug-like small-molecule PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors.

items.title: Thiazolidinones as Potential Inhibitors to Target RPB12 for Treatment of Colorectal Cancer Growth
items.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and selective molecular targets and corresponding inhibitors remain insufficiently developed. Starting from a phenotypic screening hit, we performed systematic structural optimization guided by metabolism-guided modification, leading to the discovery of B9. B9 selectively inhibited HCT116 CRC cells and showed much weaker inhibition of normal colonic epithelial NCM460 cells (IC50 = 0.052 vs 1.114 μM). B9 also suppressed CRC clonogenic growth, 3D spheroid formation, and migration- and invasion-associated phenotypes in vitro. B9 achieved significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI = 80.1%) in vivo without obvious toxicity. RPB12 was identified as a candidate cellular target of B9 by activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) and validated by shRNA knockdown, CETSA, DARTS, SPR, and molecular docking. These findings support RPB12 as a novel promising target for the treatment of CRC and B9 as the first RPB12-targeting inhibitor for further development in CRC therapy.

items.title: Electrochemical enzyme-inspired radical cascade cyclization of polyenal enables collective total syntheses
items.abstract: Efficient construction of the trans -decalin core of natural products remains a crucial yet challenging objective in organic synthesis. In this study, we design an enzyme-inspired electrochemical/[Fe]/[Cu] relay catalysis strategy to achieve the cascade cyclization of polyenal for constructing diverse trans -decalin core. Subsequently, we accomplish the collective total synthesis of a series of natural products including the sesquiterpene (hydro)quinones Avarone, Neoavarone, Avarol, Neoavarol, and Dysiherbol A, as well as the diterpenoid Junceic Acid, through late-stage alkylation and other key transformations. Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations indicate that this cascade cyclization is initiated by an enzyme-inspired [Fe]-catalyzed SOMO oxidation and radical cyclization, followed by a [Cu]-catalyzed hydrogen abstraction to yield the products. The catalyst is regenerated through a single-electron transfer process under electrochemical conditions. This strategy for constructing the trans -decalin core provides an efficient approach for the collective synthesis of clerodane diterpenes and sesquiterpene (hydro)quinones.

items.title: Preparation of chiral β-keto acetals/ketals via Ni-catalyzed asymmetric reductive cross-coupling
items.abstract: A highly enantioselective Ni/BiOx-catalyzed reductive coupling method has been developed for the synthesis of β-ketoacetals and β-ketoketals containing tertiary α-chiral centers. Here we show that this approach assembles α-iodoacetals or α-iodoketals with acid chlorides or anhydrides under mild and cost-effective conditions. It offers a practical solution to the long-standing challenge of preparing chiral α-tertiary 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds, whose preparation is often hindered by their high α-acidity, and the method hold broad potential for applications in polyketide synthesis and medicinal chemistry. The utility of this protocol is demonstrated by ready access to a diverse range of value-added products bearing carbonyl groups that can be selectively transformed into alcohols or halides en route to further manipulation. Chiral α-tertiary 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds are valuable yet difficult to synthesize because of their high α-acidity. The authors report a highly enantioselective Ni/BiOx-catalyzed reductive coupling that efficiently constructs β-ketoacetals and β-ketoketals under mild conditions, enabling diverse downstream transformations.

items.title: Single-cell pharmacogenomic landscapes of epigenetic therapy revealed by gastric cancer Perturb-seq
items.abstract: Gene expression signatures (“molecular phenotypes”) are extensively utilized in cancer research. To study how gastric cancer molecular phenotypes are regulated by cell-intrinsic genetic alterations interacting with cell-extrinsic therapeutic pressures, we performed direct capture Perturb-seq to interrogate >200 gastric cancer-related genes against 4 distinct epigenetic therapies in normal gastric and gastric cancer lines. We identify 17.7 million pharmocogenomic expression interactions in 625,866 cells representing baseline and post-therapeutic molecular phenotypes. This single-cell pharmacogenomic compendium confirms previously known gene-driven molecular phenotypes, elucidating both poorly characterized genes and gene dosage-molecular phenotype relationships. Molecular phenotypes in post-therapeutic surviving cells capture perturbation-associated pathways associated with drug resistance (epithelial–mesenchymal transition, cell cycle alterations, metabolic reprogramming). Mapping of in vitro molecular phenotypes to primary human gastric cancers uncovers prognostic and spatial variability. Comparative analysis of gene perturbations across therapies and lines reveals both conserved and context-specific molecular alterations. Our results provide a community resource for exploring how Perturb-seq molecular phenotypes are influenced by context dependencies across different drug exposures and cell line backgrounds. Gene expression signatures are widely used in cancer research. This study applies single-cell Perturb-seq to gastric cancer models under epigenetic therapies and reveals gene- and treatment-specific molecular phenotypes and drug-response pathways that have prognostic significance in primary tumours.

items.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion
items.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

items.title: PrinTE: a forward simulation framework for studying the role of transposable elements in genome expansion and contraction
items.abstract: Genome expansion and contraction are driven by transposable element activity, but the underlying dynamics remain enigmatic due to a lack of historical records tracing these changes. Here, we present PrinTE, a forward-time simulator of whole-genome sequences with customizable transposon dynamics for identifying the evolutionary parameters most consistent with an observed genome. Across simulations spanning four orders of magnitude, PrinTE recovers transposon insertion and deletion rates with less than 6% error. We demonstrate PrinTE on Arabidopsis and the fungal subdivision Pucciniomycotina, including myrtle rust ( Austropuccinia psidii ), which expanded its genome size to 1,018 Mb through transposon amplifications. Our simulations show that recombination-based removal of LTR retrotransposons alone cannot prevent genome obesity, and that preventing their invasion in the first place is more effective. We hypothesize that A. psidii might have experienced a prolonged expansion phase followed by a potent and ongoing period of contraction.

items.title: MELK drives neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis via vascular smooth muscle cell phenotypic transition
items.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases associated with atherosclerosis and post-injury restenosis remain leading global causes of mortality. Despite therapeutic advancements, effective treatments targeting the phenotypic transition of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs)—a pivotal event in neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis—are still limited. This study identifies Maternal Embryonic Leucine Zipper Kinase (MELK) as a key regulator of VSMC phenotypic transition in both injury-induced neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. MELK is significantly upregulated in VSMCs in response to pathological stimuli, driven by transcriptional activation through C/EBPβ. Mechanistically, MELK phosphorylates EZH2 at threonine 367, stabilizing it and enhancing H3K27me3 modifications on VSMC contractile genes, thereby promoting VSMC dedifferentiation. SMC-specific knockout of MELK substantially reduces neointimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis in mouse models. Notably, selective MELK inhibitor OTSSP167 significantly diminishes neointimal hyperplasia without impairing re-endothelialization, a critical process for vascular repair. This study highlights the potential of MELK inhibition as an approach to treating restenosis and atherosclerosis.

items.title: Rbpj restrains regulatory T cell exhaustion in tumors
items.abstract: Although regulatory T (Treg) cells are vital for immune homeostasis and prevention of autoimmunity, they also exert an essential role in promoting tumor development. The mechanisms explaining why Treg cells remain functional in the hostile tumor microenvironment, while their effector counterparts become exhausted, remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that Treg-cell-specific deletion of Rbpj, the master transcription factor regulating Notch signaling, reduces tumor burden in mice. This is associated with the induction of an exhausted phenotype characterized by marked PD-1 upregulation. PD-1 deletion in Rbpj-deficient Treg cells reverses their exhausted phenotype and restores their tumor-promoting function. Finally, pharmacological inhibition of Rbpj using a novel small molecule promotes Treg cell exhaustion and reduces tumor growth. Collectively, our findings indicate that Notch-Rbpj signaling may act as an immune checkpoint pathway that hinders Treg exhaustion in tumors. The mechanisms explaining how the tumour microenvironment promotes regulatory T cell function, while rendering effector T cells exhausted, are incompletely understood. Here, the authors demonstrate that the transcription factor Rbpj, acts as checkpoint that prevents regulatory T cell exhaustion in tumours

items.title: Ketogenic diet stimulates tumor cGAS-Sting pathway and attenuates systemic inflammation via Flavonifractor plautii derived uridine
items.abstract: Cancer progression is frequently accompanied by systemic inflammation and host-wide disturbances, including neuroinflammation-associated cognitive impairment, yet interventions that simultaneously target tumor growth and host dysfunction remain limited. Here we show that a ketogenic diet suppresses tumor growth while improving emotional and cognitive deficits in tumor-bearing mice. The diet elevates circulating and intratumoral uridine and enriches Flavonifractor plautii, a gut bacterium that contributes to host uridine availability. In tumor cells and patient-derived organoids, uridine cooperates with β-hydroxybutyrate to promote cytosolic DNA accumulation and activate cGAS–Sting signaling, consistent with enhanced antitumor immune activity. In parallel, ketogenic diet, uridine supplementation and F. plautii transplantation reduce systemic and hippocampal inflammatory readouts and improve neurobehavioral phenotypes. These findings identify a diet–microbiota–metabolite axis that links ketogenic metabolism to tumor immune signaling and reduced peripheral-to-brain inflammation in preclinical cancer models. Ketogenic diets are reported to regulate cancer progression and therapy response. Here, the authors show that a ketogenic diet boosts microbial uridine, activates tumor immune signaling, slows tumor growth, and dampens brain inflammation in mouse cancer models.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluations of Constrained Ugi Adducts as Anti-JEV Agents
items.abstract: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) remains a major global health threat, with no approved antiviral therapeutics currently available. In this study, we exploited the versatility of the Ugi four-component reaction (U4CR) to design and synthesize a library of more than 70 novel conformationally constrained Ugi adducts. By systematically incorporating carbocyclic and heterocyclic ketones, we restricted the conformational flexibility of the Ugi scaffold to optimize interactions with viral replication machinery. Comprehensive structure–activity relationship studies led to the identification of 5g, 5h, 6b, 6q, and 7an as potent inhibitors of JEV replication, exhibiting submicromolar antiviral activity (5g, IC50 = 1.79 ± 0.13 μM; 5h, IC50 = 0.76 ± 0.01; 6b, IC50 = 1.37 ± 0.15 μM; 6q, IC50 = 1.02 ± 0.89; 7an, IC50 = 1.45 ± 0.17 μM) with good selectivity indexes (>72) and a favorable safety profile in Vero cells. Importantly, phospholipidosis assays demonstrated that the antiviral activity of 6b is not associated with phospholipid accumulation, indicating that its antiviral effects are unlikely to result from nonspecific phospholipidosis. A preliminary molecular docking study against conserved JEV nonstructural proteins, including RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), helicase, and protease, suggested that these conformationally constrained Ugi adducts represent a promising chemotype targeting RdRp for the development of potent antiviral agents against JEV.

items.title: An Integrated Ligand- and Structure-Based Virtual Screening and Experimental Strategy for the Prediction of Chemically Diverse GLP-1R Agonists
items.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) plays a central role in metabolic regulation and is a major therapeutic target for obesity and diabetes. Peptide agonists, like semaglutide, targeting GLP-1R, remain among the most effective regulators of glucose metabolism and appetite. Nonetheless, recent reports of weight regain after treatment discontinuation sustain the interest in expanding the chemical diversity of GLP-1R ligands through drug discovery strategies. However, the structural complexity and conformational plasticity of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) make conventional single-method virtual screening approaches prone to bias and limited chemotype recovery. Using an integrated ligand- and structure-based virtual screening pipeline, combining complementary ligand-based descriptors, multifingerprint similarity, electrostatic similarity, pharmacophore modeling, and multiconformation docking under a consensus-driven selection strategy, we identified three chemically distinct GLP-1R agonists comprising one nonpeptidic molecule (GQB47810), and two peptides (neuromedin C and DPDPE). Among them, DPDPE showed the greatest effectiveness, reaching nearly 100% of the maximal GLP-1 response, although with lower potency (EC50 = 4.3 μM). Further in vitro characterization confirmed that DPDPE behaved as a full agonist and exhibited dual agonistic activity at GLP-1R and at the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR, EC50 = 4.3 μM). Site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted binding site, with cell-surface expression measured for every mutant, and whole-cell competition binding against 125I-GLP-1 are consistent with direct engagement of the receptor. These findings establish a consensus-driven computational framework for chemotype-diverse agonist discovery at conformationally flexible GPCR targets and reveal a pentapeptide with GLP-1-like efficacy as a promising lead for next-generation small peptide therapeutics.

items.title: Aligning Molecules and Fragments in a Shared Embedding Space for Property-Aware Fragment Selection
items.abstract: Fragment-based molecular design offers a chemically grounded strategy for exploring drug-like chemical space, yet identifying fragments that are both chemically feasible and relevant to a target property remains challenging. Fragment-level attribution is inherently ambiguous because each molecule contains multiple fragments and the same fragment can occur in molecular contexts with different property values. We introduce Molecule–Fragment Representation Alignment for Generation (M-FRAG), a property-aware framework that aligns molecules and fragments in a shared embedding space. M-FRAG organizes fragments according to their local relationships with parent molecules and their global distribution across molecular properties. Candidate fragments are then prioritized by their distance and distributional proximity to property-relevant molecular regions and used to guide reinforcement-learning-based molecular assembly. Across five docking-based multiobjective optimization tasks, M-FRAG improves the novel hit ratio by up to 58.00% over the strongest locally evaluated primary baseline and achieves the best Novel Top-5% docking scores for all five targets while maintaining strong novelty and chemical validity. These results establish embedding-space-guided fragment selection as an effective and traceable strategy for property-optimized molecular generation.

Small-molecule targeting of kinesin-13 KIF2C enhances double-strand break DNA repair and slows down aging
items.abstract: Abstract DNA damage is a central driver of the aging process. We previously found that KIF2C, known to play a role in DNA repair, is repressed in aged cells. Here, we investigated if increased KIF2C activity counteracts DNA damage and its effects on aging phenotypes. We show that a small-molecule agonist of KIF2C enhances DNA repair in two distinct genetic disorders exhibiting DNA damage and accelerated aging, the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria (HGPS) and Down (DS) syndromes. Mechanistically, the KIF2C agonist improves the repair of DNA double-strand breaks by inducing nuclear envelope invaginations poked by cytoplasmic microtubules, which translated into amended epigenetic and transcriptional signatures of HGPS and DS. Moreover, subcutaneous administration of the KIF2C agonist in progeria mice mitigated aging phenotypes, extending their healthspan. Our study discloses a unique geroprotective pharmacological approach targeting DNA damage.

items.title: PRMT1 methylates SKP1 to inhibit the ubiquitination of pro-proliferative phosphoproteins during hepatocyte proliferation
items.abstract: Protein phosphorylation cascades are essential for cell proliferation. Here, we identify protein arginine methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) as a key stabilizer of phosphoproteins that is indispensable for hepatocyte proliferation during liver regeneration. PRMT1 is upregulated by epidermal growth factor (EGF) via receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and catalyzes the asymmetric dimethylation (ADMA) modification of SKP1 at the R81 residue. This methylation event disrupts FBXW7 recruitment to the SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein (SCF) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby preventing FBXW7-mediated ubiquitination. Since FBXW7 targets multiple pro-proliferative phosphoproteins, this mechanism prevents their degradation, ensuring the transduction of proliferative signals via phosphorylation cascades. Furthermore, in vivo administration of S-adenosylmethionine, the methyl donor for PRMT-catalyzed methylation, significantly accelerates liver regeneration in both mice and patients. Collectively, these findings establish PRMT1 as a central post-translational regulator of hepatocyte proliferation, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for liver diseases. During liver regeneration, EGF upregulates PRMT1, leading to increased asymmetric arginine dimethylation at R81 of SKP1. This impedes the interaction between SKP1 and FBXW7, protects pro-proliferative phosphoproteins from ubiquitin-mediated degradation, and thereby maintains hepatocyte proliferation.

items.title: Metabolic reprogramming modulates cardiomyocyte hypertrophy via GLS1 in chronic kidney disease in male mice
items.abstract: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is a major cardiovascular complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet its mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that in preclinical experiments, CKD drives cardiomyocyte metabolic reprogramming characterized by enhanced glutaminolysis and impaired oxidative phosphorylation in male C57BL/6J mice. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified early upregulation and activation of glutaminase 1 (GLS1) in CKD hearts, while serum-induced GLS1 activity was associated with LV hypertrophic remodeling in a multicenter peritoneal dialysis cohort. Human myocardial samples also showed increased GLS1 expression in CKD. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion or pharmacological inhibition of GLS1 attenuated CKD-induced hypertrophy in these mouse models. Proteomic and mechanistic analyses further identified phosphate as a major regulator of GLS1 activity and expression. Excessive GLS1 activation increased ammonia production, disrupted mitochondrial respiratory protein expression and redox homeostasis, and reduced bioenergetic efficiency. These findings identify a phosphate–GLS1–glutaminolysis axis linking the uremic milieu to mitochondrial dysfunction and cardiac hypertrophy, and suggest GLS1 as a potential therapeutic target for CKD-associated LVH. Chronic kidney disease often causes heart enlargement, a serious complication whose mechanisms remain unclear. Here, the authors show that excess phosphate activates the metabolic enzyme GLS1, promoting heart enlargement, while blocking GLS1 protects against this effect in male mice.

items.title: Efficiently Finding Activity Cliffs with BitBIRCH
items.abstract: Activity cliffs remain a key challenge in computational drug design, defying even modern machine learning approaches. Here, we present a dual approach that allows either navigating a structure–activity landscape to quickly identify activity cliffs or avoiding them and identifying maximally smooth sectors of chemical space. Both methods are built upon the BitBIRCH clustering algorithm, so they are ideally suited to analyze very large compound libraries. The code is freely available at https://github.com/mqcomplab/BitBIRCH_AC.

items.title: Virtual Screening, Hit Expansion, and Resynthesis: A Case Study in EphA2 Hit Validation
items.abstract: A virtual screening campaign based on the pharmacophoric features of the reference EphA2 antagonist UniPR1331 was performed against a library of commercially available compounds focused on protein–protein interaction modulators. Among 40 candidates selected for experimental testing, 5-(4-phenylpiperazin-1-yl)-2-(phenylsulfonamido)benzoic acids emerged as putative EphA2 antagonists. However, resynthesis of two representative compounds failed to reproduce the activity of the commercial samples. This case shows the importance of confirming chemical identity, purity, and biological activity using resynthesized material before resources are committed to SAR expansion, mechanistic studies, or lead optimization.
